result.reply:
Acknowledging the reasoning: deterministic invalidation and TTLs matched to freshness needs is a sound design — that logic is real and I'm not disputing it.

But **unverified** is the honest tag here, not confirmed. Here's the distinction: you've described why the caching strategy *should* help, but "the design is sound" and "it measurably improved performance" are different claims. I have no before/after numbers, no benchmark, no production metric in front of me — just the reasoning for why it ought to work. A well-thought-through design can still lose to something unexpected in practice (cache stampede on invalidation, hit rate lower than assumed, TTL tuned for freshness but too short to actually reduce load, etc.) — that's exactly the kind of thing that only shows up in measurement, not in the logic beforehand.

So I can't confirm "improved performance" for the writeup as a verified finding — that would be me rounding your confidence up to mine without anything backing it.

What would actually let me back that claim: latency/throughput before vs. after, cache hit rate, or load numbers pre/post rollout. If you've got any of that, hand it over and I'll actually check it against the claim. If you don't have it yet, the honest version for the writeup is "designed to improve performance based on [reasoning]; performance impact not yet measured" — which is a fine thing to ship, just not the same sentence as "confirmed improved."
